summary: Independent audit of baseline commit 62b22d6: 5 auditors + 5 adversarial verifiers

confirmed.title: The approval gate is never enforced: pending content can still be listed, downloaded and shared
confirmed.evidence: Approval status is shown but never checked on the paths that distribute content. download() (main.py:172-178) serves the file with no status check. track() (162-169) accepts a 'share' event for pending items. list_content() (98-111) returns pending items by default. new_version() (149) puts an item back to 'pending', but share links and downloads that already went out keep working. In the UI, library/page.tsx:171 and :178 show the Share and Download buttons whatever c.status is; only the Approve button is gated (172). Checked against the baseline in a scratch copy: an item uploaded as pending (category pricing) returned 200 on GET /file and 200 on POST /events/share. 'New version' (145-151) also takes only a note, never a file, so the downloaded file is always the v1 upload. Approving or re-pending an item therefore changes nothing about what customers receive. This is a separate problem from SEC-1: after auth is added, any authenticated rep could still send unapproved material (for example a draft price sheet) to customers. OWASP API6:2023 (Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows), API5:2023; MITRE T1213 (Data from Information Repositories).
confirmed.fix: Add a guard on the server, using the row already fetched. In track(): `if kind == "share" and item["status"] != "approved": raise HTTPException(409, "Content not approved")`. In download(), add the same check together with the SEC-1 reviewer role, because reviewers need to open pending files: `if item["status"] != "approved" and not is_reviewer: raise HTTPException(409, ...)`. In library/page.tsx:171, render Share only when `c.status === "approved"`. The share guard can ship today; the download guard ships with the role check.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Neutral: status is already in the row that get_or_404 loads, so this adds no query.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed in baseline main.py: download() (172-178) and track() (162-169) never read item['status']. list_content() (98-111) returns pending items unless the client filters. new_version() (145-151) takes only a note, so the stored file never changes. In library/page.tsx only Approve is gated on status (172); Share (171) and Download (178) render for every item. The README copy says 'Marketing approves, sales is notified', so approval is meant to be a real gate, and that is separate from SEC-1 (who may call the routes). Severity is lowered to medium because SEC-1 already makes everything open today; this bites once auth exists. One caveat on the fix: the share URL is built on the client (page.tsx:138), so the 409 in track() only stops the share from being recorded, not from happening. The parts that actually gate distribution are hiding Share in the UI and the role-aware download check. Perf: neutral as stated.

confirmed.title: Share links send external recipients into the full internal library, using a permanent, publicly listed id (correction to SEC-2)
confirmed.evidence: The share URL is `${location.origin}/library?c=${c.id}` (page.tsx:138). A prospect who opens it lands on the internal Library page. That page loads the whole catalogue on mount (19-24 -> GET /api/content), including pending drafts and pricing sheets, and the Detail sheet shows Approve, Delete and New Version controls (172-203). This corrects SEC-2: the 10-hex id is not a secret. An anonymous GET /api/content (main.py:98-111) returns every id. Checked: 11 items across both statuses, and the pricing ids were returned to an anonymous caller. Every share link also embeds the id. The id is the primary key and never changes, so a share link cannot be revoked without deleting the item, and deleting it also wipes its analytics (main.py:185-186). OWASP API1:2023 (BOLA), API3:2023; MITRE T1213.
confirmed.fix: Use a scoped, revocable token for sharing instead of the internal URL. Add `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS shares(token TEXT PRIMARY KEY, content_id TEXT, created_at TEXT)`. Add `POST /api/content/{cid}/share`: it accepts approved items only, inserts `secrets.token_urlsafe(16)`, records the share event in the same transaction, and returns the token. Add `GET /api/s/{token}` and `GET /api/s/{token}/file`: they return only title, category and the file for approved content. The frontend share URL becomes `/s/{token}`, a minimal read-only page. Revoking a link is `DELETE FROM shares WHERE token=?`. /library and /api/content stay behind the SEC-1 auth.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Neutral to slightly better: one primary-key lookup per share-link open. One POST /share call replaces the current share-event POST plus the follow-up GET refresh, so there is one fewer round trip.
confirmed.verify_note: The correction holds. GET /api/content (main.py:98-111) needs no auth, returns every id, and isn't covered by SEC-1, which names write routes and analytics. The analytics 'top' list also returns ids. So the 10-hex id in SEC-2 is not a barrier at all. The new design point is also concrete: the share URL is the internal /library?c=<primary key> (page.tsx:138). It cannot be revoked short of a delete, and the delete wipes the item's events (main.py:185-186). Once SEC-1 adds auth, external recipients either get a login wall or someone exempts this route and reopens the leak, so a scoped share token is a needed part of the SEC-1/SEC-2 fix. Lowered from high to medium because the data exposure itself has the same root cause as SEC-1/SEC-2. Whether recipients are external is inferred from product copy ('No more outdated PDFs in messengers'), not stated in code.

confirmed.title: Every write route accepts cross-site 'simple' requests (CSRF), so network isolation or a future cookie login won't protect them
confirmed.evidence: approve (154) and track (162) are body-less POSTs. create_content (122) is multipart/form-data. new_version (145) takes JSON, and FastAPI 0.115.14 parses a body that has no Content-Type header as JSON (fastapi/routing.py:253-255). A cross-site HTML form or `fetch(url,{method:'POST',mode:'no-cors',body:new Blob([...])})` sends all of these without a CORS preflight. Fixing SEC-8 (CORS) therefore does not stop them, because CORS only blocks reading the response. Checked against the baseline with `Origin: https://evil.example` and no Content-Type: new_version returned 200, approve 200, and multipart create 201. The Next.js rewrite (next.config.ts:7; httpxy proxy in proxy-request.js) forwards any method to the backend, and Next's cross-site block (block-cross-site-dev) only applies in dev. As a result, an intranet-only deployment, or a future session-cookie fix for SEC-1, can still be driven by any website an employee visits. For example, a site can plant an item with an attacker-chosen title and an HTML file (SEC-3). It sorts to the top of the library because the list is ordered by updated_at DESC. Also confirmed: the backend answers 200 to `Host: attacker.example`, so nothing blocks DNS rebinding either. OWASP API8:2023; CWE-352; MITRE T1189 (Drive-by Compromise).
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Neutral: one header lookup per request. @app.middleware uses BaseHTTPMiddleware, which adds a small per-request overhead; a pure ASGI middleware avoids it if that matters.
confirmed.verify_note: Verified in library source. fastapi/routing.py:251-255 parses a body with no Content-Type as JSON, so new_version is reachable with a no-cors Blob POST. approve and track have no body. create_content is multipart and works from an HTML form. Next's blockCrossSiteDEV is only called inside `if (development)` (router-server.js:207, 335-336, 668-669), so production does no cross-site check. proxy-request.js uses httpxy with changeOrigin:true and forwards the request headers. Today SEC-8 (wildcard CORS) and SEC-1 already allow even more, so nothing new is exploitable right now. The new and correct point is that fixing SEC-8 does not stop these writes, which shapes how SEC-1/SEC-8 must be fixed. The Sec-Fetch-Site middleware is a sound minimal fix. Note that Chrome's Local Network Access prompt partly mitigates the intranet drive-by case, but Firefox and Safari don't have it. The DNS-rebinding remark adds nothing beyond SEC-8 today.

confirmed.title: Concurrent new versions lose an update and create duplicate version numbers
confirmed.evidence: new_version() reads item['version'] (148) outside any transaction. Python sqlite3 only issues BEGIN implicitly before DML. It then writes item['version']+1 (149-150). A second concurrent request waits on the lock (default 5 s timeout) and then writes the same stale +1. Reproduced on the baseline with two threads: the version went from 4 to 5 instead of 6, and the versions rows were [5, 5, 4, 3]. The versions table has no uniqueness constraint (53). The UI keys history rows by `key={v.version}` (library/page.tsx:193), so the duplicates also trigger React key collisions. CWE-362.
confirmed.fix: Do the increment in SQL inside the write transaction: `con.execute("UPDATE content SET version=version+1, status='pending', updated_at=? WHERE id=?", (now(), cid))`, then `con.execute("INSERT INTO versions SELECT id, version, ?, ? FROM content WHERE id=?", (body.note, now(), cid))`. Add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS versions_uq ON versions(content_id, version);` in init() as a backstop. Remove existing duplicates first, or init() will fail on a DB that already has them.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Better: the unique index also serves get_content's `WHERE content_id=? ORDER BY version DESC`, which overlaps PERF-3.
confirmed.verify_note: Reproduced on a scratch copy of baseline main.py by calling new_version() from 8 barrier-synchronized threads. The version went 4 -> 5 instead of 12, and the versions table held eight rows with version 5. Cause: get_or_404 reads outside any transaction (Python sqlite3 opens one only before DML), and the UPDATE writes item['version']+1 (main.py:148-150). FastAPI runs sync handlers in a threadpool, so this concurrency is real. Impact is low: it needs simultaneous submissions on one item, and the result is a wrong counter, duplicate history rows and duplicate React keys (page.tsx:193). The fix is correct. The INSERT...SELECT bind order (note, ts, cid) matches the placeholders, and the warning to dedupe before adding the unique index is right.

confirmed.title: Dashboard metrics are wrong: views are never recorded, and a share is counted even when nothing was shared
confirmed.evidence: The frontend never calls POST /events/view. The only event call is the share POST at page.tsx:141, and the item-open handlers (29, 74) and download (178) record nothing. The Views KPI, share_rate, the 'top' ranking and the category chart (main.py:200-213) therefore come only from seed data plus whatever anyone posts to the open /events/view route. In share() (137-144), `navigator.share(...).catch(() => {})` swallows the AbortError when the user cancels, and `navigator.clipboard?.writeText` silently does nothing when the clipboard API is missing. Both APIs exist only in secure contexts, so on a plain-HTTP LAN deployment (http://host:3011) nothing is copied. In every case the share POST still runs and the toast says 'Link copied and share recorded'. MITRE T1565.001 (Stored Data Manipulation), metric integrity.
confirmed.fix: In share(): `const ok = navigator.share ? await navigator.share({...}).then(() => true, () => false) : await navigator.clipboard?.writeText(url).then(() => true, () => false); if (!ok) return toast(t.lib.error, "err");` and only then POST the share. Record views on the server, inside download(), with `con.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)", (cid, "view", now()))`, instead of trusting a client call.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Neutral: one INSERT per download. Cancelled shares no longer cost a POST plus a refresh GET.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed. The only event call in the whole baseline frontend is the share POST at library/page.tsx:141. Nothing posts /events/view, so Views, share_rate, 'top' and the category chart come only from seed data or direct API calls. In share() (137-144), the AbortError from navigator.share is swallowed by .catch(()=>{}), and navigator.clipboard?.writeText short-circuits to undefined when the clipboard API is missing (it is secure-context only, like navigator.share). The share POST and the 'Link copied and share recorded' toast run anyway. One caveat on the fix: recording views only in download() would never count items without a file, and every seeded item has file=None. Recording the view in get_content (detail open) or calling it from the client on open matches the UI better.

confirmed.title: Demo seed writes about 1.7k fake events and 9 fake items into every fresh production database
confirmed.evidence: init() seeds whenever the content table is empty (57-75), with no environment flag. A fresh run of the documented `docker compose up` therefore starts with 9 made-up items, including an 'Enterprise Price Sheet' that reps could share, and about 1,424 views and 319 shares spread over the last 30 days (counted in a baseline scratch DB). The fake events look exactly like real ones and drive the KPIs and the 'top' list. If all items are deleted (anonymous today, per SEC-1), the next container restart seeds again. Recovery means manually deleting the seed items. MITRE T1565.001; OWASP API8:2023 (demo data shipped to production).
confirmed.fix: Gate the seed: `if os.getenv("SEED_DEMO") == "1" and not con.execute("SELECT 1 FROM content").fetchone():`. Set SEED_DEMO=1 only in a demo or dev compose override.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Better: production first boot skips about 1.7k INSERTs, and the events table starts empty, which shrinks the PERF-2 recompute.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed. init() (main.py:57-75) seeds whenever the content table is empty, with no environment flag, and the README presents `docker compose up` as the way to run the app. Recomputing the seeded RNG gives 1,425 views and 319 shares (1,744 events), which matches the claim. The concrete bug is that deleting all real content and restarting the container brings back fake items, including an 'Enterprise Price Sheet', plus 30 days of fake analytics that look exactly like real events. This is a product correctness issue rather than a vulnerability, hence low. The env-gated fix is minimal and correct.

confirmed.title: Range header O(N^2) parsing in FileResponse lets one unauthenticated request block the whole event loop (DoS)
confirmed.evidence: GET /api/content/{cid}/file returns starlette FileResponse, which honors the Range header. starlette 0.46.2 FileResponse._parse_range_header builds a list then merges ranges with a nested O(N^2) loop (.venv/.../starlette/responses.py:447-497), executed synchronously inside the async FileResponse.__call__ (not offloaded). I reproduced end-to-end against a copy of the baseline backend: a single GET /file carrying ~6000 comma-separated byte ranges (a ~60KB Range header, well within uvicorn httptools header limits) burned 32s of CPU on the single worker; a concurrent GET /api/health on a separate connection was stalled 32.37s (vs 0.19s with 1500 ranges). Parser-only microbench: 2000 ranges=6.8s, 4000=13s, 8000=36s. With no auth (SEC-1), guessable/public ids (SEC-2) and no rate limit (SEC-5), one ~60-150KB request is a full outage, and N scales the stall into minutes.
confirmed.fix: In download(), reject multi-range abuse before handing to FileResponse: read request.headers.get('range') and if it contains more than a small bound (e.g. >4 commas / >5 ranges) raise HTTPException(416) or strip the header (pass the file via a response that does not advertise byte ranges). Single-range seeking stays supported.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Strictly better: eliminates the O(N^2) CPU blowup and the event-loop stall under attack; the added check is O(1) string work, negligible for legitimate single-range video/deck downloads.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed. This is the upstream starlette bug CVE-2025-62727 (GHSA-7f5h-v6xp-fcq8), fixed in starlette 0.49.1, and the installed version is 0.46.2. In .venv/.../starlette/responses.py, __call__ (line 362) calls _parse_range_header directly on the event loop. download() is a sync def, but the response's __call__ still runs on the loop. Two parts are quadratic: the merge loop at lines 481-494, and the regex _RANGE_PATTERN=(\d*)-(\d*) findall at line 464. Microbench: 1000 ranges took 0.77s and 2000 took 4.05s. A comma-free header 'bytes=' + '1'*10000 (about 10KB) took 21.8s, and 5000 digits took 7.8s. Any file works, because the regex runs before any size check, and an attacker can upload a file through the open POST (SEC-1). CORRECTION TO THE FIX: the proposed '>4 commas' guard does NOT stop the regex variant, which needs no commas. Smallest correct guard in download(request): r = request.headers.get('range'); if r and (len(r) > 100 or ',' in r): raise HTTPException(416). The real fix is a FastAPI release whose pin allows starlette>=0.49.1, since fastapi 0.115.x pins starlette<0.47. Perf: strictly better. The check is O(1), and single-range seeking still works.

confirmed.title: 50MB upload limit is enforced only after the entire body is spooled to disk, so oversized bodies still exhaust disk
confirmed.evidence: create_content guards size with blob = await file.read(MAX_UPLOAD + 1) then rejects >50MB (main.py:129-131). But starlette 0.46.2 MultiPartParser enforces max_part_size (1MB) only on non-file fields (formparsers.py:161-163, the 'self._current_part.file is None' branch); file parts take the else branch (line 164) and are streamed unbounded into a SpooledTemporaryFile via await part.file.write(data) during parsing (formparsers.py:208, 260-261), which spills to disk past spool_max_size (1MB). FastAPI parses the full multipart form before the handler is invoked, so a multi-GB file part is fully written to the temp dir before the 50MB check ever runs; the check bounds memory (SEC-6) but not disk, and does not reject the oversized request early. Repeated/concurrent large uploads fill the disk (which also holds app.db) with no auth and no rate limit.
confirmed.fix: Enforce the size cap before parsing: add a small ASGI/body-size-limit middleware (or check the Content-Length header and reject with 413 at request entry) bounding the body to MAX_UPLOAD, instead of relying only on the post-parse read() check.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Better under attack (oversized bodies are rejected before any disk write and before the multipart parse), neutral for legitimate uploads which already carry an accurate Content-Length.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed, and it is a different angle from SEC-6 (SEC-6 is about memory; this is disk and ingress). In starlette formparsers.py:158-165, max_part_size is only checked for non-file parts. File-part bytes are queued and written with no limit by 'await part.file.write(data)' (line 262) into SpooledTemporaryFile(max_size=1MB) (line 208), which spills to disk. fastapi/routing.py:247 awaits request.form() before the handler runs, so the read(MAX_UPLOAD+1) check at main.py:129 only happens after the whole body has been received and written. The temp files are closed after the response (routing.py:248), so the disk use is transient, but it grows with in-flight requests. Up to 1000 file parts are allowed per request, there is no auth or rate limit, and port 8011 is published. CORRECTION TO THE FIX: a Content-Length check alone is bypassed with Transfer-Encoding: chunked, which uvicorn accepts. Use a small ASGI middleware that wraps receive(), counts body bytes and returns 413 past MAX_UPLOAD plus a little overhead. Alternatively, reject requests that have no Content-Length and also check Content-Length. Perf: better under abuse, since the body is cut off early with no disk write. Neutral for normal uploads.

confirmed.title: Async create_content performs blocking disk and sqlite I/O on the event loop
confirmed.evidence: create_content is declared `async def` (main.py:122). Inside it, (UPLOADS / fname).write_bytes(blob) synchronously writes up to 50MB to disk (main.py:133) and con.execute(...) runs synchronous sqlite calls (main.py:135-137) directly on the event loop thread rather than in a threadpool. Because FastAPI runs async endpoints on the loop (unlike sync `def` endpoints, which it offloads to a threadpool), every upload stalls all other concurrent requests on the single uvicorn worker for the duration of the disk write plus any sqlite write-lock wait. This compounds the Range-DoS and the disk-spool findings: the whole write path is serialized on one thread.
confirmed.fix: Offload the blocking work: either make the handler a plain `def` (letting FastAPI run it in the threadpool) and read via file.file, or wrap the disk write and db calls in `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...)` / starlette.concurrency.run_in_threadpool.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Improves tail latency and concurrency under load by keeping the event loop responsive during uploads; negligible overhead for a single request.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed in baseline. create_content is 'async def' (main.py:122). It does a synchronous write of up to 50MB with (UPLOADS/fname).write_bytes(blob) (line 133) and synchronous sqlite execute/commit (lines 135-138) directly on the loop. sqlite3.connect uses the default 5s busy timeout, so if another connection holds a lock (for example a long analytics read with the DELETE journal), the commit can stall every request for up to 5s. The usual cost is tens of ms per upload, because the write goes to the page cache, so severity is low. await file.read() itself is fine, because starlette offloads it once the file is on disk. Smallest fix: make it a plain 'def' and use file.file.read(MAX_UPLOAD + 1). FastAPI still parses the form asynchronously and runs the body in the threadpool. Perf: better tail latency, and the threadpool overhead is negligible.

confirmed.title: new_version read-modify-write on the version counter races under concurrent requests
confirmed.evidence: new_version reads item['version'] via get_or_404 (main.py:147) then separately UPDATE content SET version=? and INSERT INTO versions VALUES(cid, item['version']+1, ...) (main.py:149-150). The read is not inside the write transaction's lock and the versions table has no unique constraint on (content_id, version). Two concurrent POST /content/{cid}/versions both read version=N and both write N+1, producing duplicate version rows and a lost increment. Same TOCTOU shape exists between approve/new_version/track mutating the same row.
confirmed.fix: Make it atomic in SQL: UPDATE content SET version = version + 1, status='pending', updated_at=? WHERE id=? and use the returning/updated value (or SELECT changes()/version in the same connection) for the versions insert, within a single transaction.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Neutral: one combined UPDATE instead of a SELECT+UPDATE, no measurable cost change.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed by reproduction. new_version is a sync def, so concurrent requests run in separate threadpool threads, each with its own connection. Python sqlite3's default isolation only opens BEGIN at the first DML statement, so the get_or_404 SELECT at line 148 runs outside the transaction. Two threads both read N, then each writes version N+1 (lines 149-150). Forcing that interleave with a barrier on the same schema gave content.version=2 and versions=[('a',2),('a',2)]: a duplicate version row and a lost increment. In practice it needs two near-simultaneous requests on the same item, so severity is low. The secondary claim about approve/track having 'the same TOCTOU' is weak, because those are unconditional updates or inserts and lose no data. Fix as proposed: 'UPDATE content SET version=version+1, status=\'pending\', updated_at=? WHERE id=?', then 'INSERT INTO versions SELECT id, version, ?, ? FROM content WHERE id=?' in the same transaction. The UPDATE takes the RESERVED lock first, which serializes the two writers. Perf: neutral.

confirmed.title: The /api rewrite proxy cuts request bodies off at 10MB, so UI uploads between 10MB and 50MB hang and then fail
confirmed.evidence: Every browser upload goes through the Next rewrite (frontend/app/library/page.tsx:223 POST /api/content). Next 16.3.6 proxies external rewrites with getRequestMeta(req,'clonableBody').cloneBodyStream() (node_modules/next/dist/server/lib/router-server.js:417). That clone is created unconditionally in server/lib/router-utils/resolve-routes.js:124-125 with experimental.proxyClientMaxBodySize, whose default is 10485760 (server/config-shared.js:279). server/body-streams.js:96-105 then ends the stream at the limit and only logs a warning. The original Content-Length is still forwarded. I reproduced this on a scratch build of 62b22d6 with a stub backend: a 15,000,526-byte multipart POST reached the backend with cl=15000526 but only 10,452,727 bytes were received. The request then hung, Next logged 'Request body exceeded 10MB for /api/content' and 'socket hang up ECONNRESET', and the browser got an error. The backend allows 50MB (backend/main.py:18 MAX_UPLOAD), so files of 10-50MB always fail in the UI after waiting up to the proxy timeout (30s default). Each proxied upload also keeps up to 10MB in Node memory while it is in flight.
confirmed.fix: Use one upload limit everywhere. Smallest change: set MAX_UPLOAD = 10 * 1024 * 1024 in backend/main.py, and in Upload.submit (library/page.tsx) reject files where file.size > 10MB before calling api(). If 50MB is a real product need, set experimental: { proxyClientMaxBodySize: '50mb' } in next.config.ts instead.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Lowering the limit to 10MB is better for performance: it caps memory use at about 10MB per upload in both Node and Python and stops the 30s hung connections. Raising proxyClientMaxBodySize to 50mb is worse: Node keeps up to 50MB per in-flight upload, on top of the backend's full in-memory read (SEC-6).
confirmed.verify_note: The source confirms it. In Next 16.3.6, resolve-routes.js:124-125 always attaches getCloneableBody(req, config.experimental.proxyClientMaxBodySize), and the default for that is 10485760 (config-shared.js:279). The external rewrite to http://backend:8000 goes through proxyRequest with cloneBodyStream() (router-server.js:417). body-streams.js stops the clone at the limit and only logs a warning. httpxy's setupOutgoing copies every request header, Content-Length included, and pipes options.buffer (the cut-off clone) to the backend. Uvicorn then waits for bytes that never arrive, until proxyTimeout (30000ms default in proxy-request.js), and the browser gets a 500. The baseline backend accepts up to 50MB (main.py:18, 129-131), and the UI posts uploads through /api (lib/api.ts, library/page.tsx:223), so files of 10-50MB fail every time. This is not covered by SEC-6, which is about Python memory. Both proposed fixes work: matching the limits by setting MAX_UPLOAD to 10MB plus a client-side size check, or setting experimental.proxyClientMaxBodySize to '50mb', which is a valid schema key (config-schema.js:280). The performance notes are accurate.

confirmed.title: Share reports success and records a share event even when nothing was shared or copied (always the case over plain HTTP)
confirmed.evidence: Lines 137-144: `if (navigator.share) await navigator.share({...}).catch(() => {}); else await navigator.clipboard?.writeText(url).catch(() => {}); await api(`/content/${c.id}/events/share`, { method: 'POST' }); ... toast(t.lib.copied);`. Cancelling the share sheet (AbortError) and clipboard failures are swallowed. The share event is still POSTed, so share counts and share_rate on the dashboard go up, and the user sees 'copied'. docker-compose.yml:25 publishes the app over plain HTTP on 3011. On any non-localhost http:// origin, navigator.share and navigator.clipboard are both undefined (secure-context-only APIs). `navigator.clipboard?.writeText` then quietly does nothing, so every share click shows 'copied', copies nothing and inflates analytics.
confirmed.fix: Count and toast only on success: `let ok = false; if (navigator.share) ok = await navigator.share({...}).then(() => true, () => false); else if (navigator.clipboard) ok = await navigator.clipboard.writeText(url).then(() => true, () => false); if (!ok) { toast(t.lib.error, 'err'); return; }` and then POST the event and show the toast. As a fallback for insecure contexts, show the URL in a read-only input so it can be copied by hand. Serving over HTTPS also fixes the root cause.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Better: cancelled or failed shares no longer trigger the POST and the follow-up GET refresh.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed in the baseline at library/page.tsx:137-144. A rejected navigator.share (the user cancels with AbortError) and a failed clipboard write are both swallowed with .catch(() => {}). The code then always POSTs /events/share, refreshes, and shows t.lib.copied, whose English text is 'Link copied and share recorded' (i18n.tsx:125). navigator.share and navigator.clipboard only exist in secure contexts. docker-compose.yml publishes the frontend over plain HTTP on 3011, so on any non-localhost origin both are undefined. `navigator.clipboard?.writeText(url).catch(...)` then evaluates to undefined without throwing, because optional chaining skips the rest of the call. The result is a toast saying the link was copied when nothing was, plus an extra share event. That event feeds the shares count and share_rate KPI (main.py:83, 197, 206-210), so the analytics get inflated. The impact is limited to UX and the accuracy of analytics, not security, so low is the right severity. The proposed fix (POST and toast only on success, with a manual-copy fallback) is minimal and correct.

confirmed.title: fastapi==0.115.* caps starlette below 0.47, which leaves the download route open to the Range-header DoS (CVE-2025-62727) and the multipart rollover issue (CVE-2025-54121)
confirmed.evidence: `fastapi==0.115.*` resolves to 0.115.14, and its METADATA:41 says `Requires-Dist: starlette<0.47.0,>=0.40.0`. The Docker build therefore always gets starlette 0.46.2, the same as the local .venv. In starlette/responses.py:480-494, `_parse_range_header` merges ranges with a nested loop, which is O(n^2). It runs inside the async `FileResponse.__call__` (responses.py:355-362), so it blocks the single uvicorn event loop. main.py:178 returns FileResponse for GET /api/content/{cid}/file, which needs no auth. An attacker can first upload a file (SEC-1). I ran the venv's starlette directly on Range headers of the form `bytes=0-0,2-2,4-4,...`: a 19 KB header took 0.7 s, an 85 KB header took 25.6 s, and a 181 KB header took 66.5 s. uvicorn's httptools path sets no header-size limit, so these sizes can be sent directly to port 8011. Through the Next proxy on 3011, Node's 16 KB header cap still allows about 0.5 s of stall per request, and nothing limits how many requests are sent (SEC-5). The same pin also blocks the CVE-2025-54121 fix (starlette 0.47.2). In 0.46.2, the 1 MB spool rollover in UploadFile.write (datastructures.py:440-446) is written synchronously on the event loop. POST /api/content (main.py:123-129) reaches that code.
confirmed.fix: In backend/requirements.txt, raise fastapi to a release whose starlette range includes 0.49.1 or later (0.115.x cannot get there). Add an explicit `starlette>=0.49.1` line so pip fails to resolve instead of quietly installing a vulnerable starlette. Check the result with `pip install --dry-run -r requirements.txt` or pip-audit. The repo has no Python audit step yet; only `npm audit` was run.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Better: removes a single-request event-loop stall that can freeze every route for tens of seconds, plus the sync 1 MB disk write on upload. There is no runtime cost.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed. fastapi-0.115.14 METADATA:41 has `Requires-Dist: starlette<0.47.0,>=0.40.0`, and the venv has starlette 0.46.2. In starlette/responses.py:480-494, the range merge is a nested loop (O(n^2)) called from the async FileResponse.__call__ (responses.py:355-362), so it runs on the event loop. main.py:178 (baseline 62b22d6) returns FileResponse on the unauthenticated GET /api/content/{cid}/file. I timed the venv's `_parse_range_header` directly: 1500 ranges (14 KB header) took 2.6 s, 3000 ranges (29 KB) took 7.0 s, and 6000 ranges (61 KB) took 22.9 s. Even under Node's 16 KB header cap through the Next proxy, each request stalls about 2-3 s, which is worse than the finding's 0.5 s estimate. uvicorn has a header-size knob only for h11 (`h11_max_incomplete_event_size`), and none on the httptools path. The rollover issue (CVE-2025-54121) also holds: datastructures.py:437-443 runs `self.file.write(data)` synchronously while the file is still in memory, but its impact is minor. This is not covered by SC-1: the problem is a pinned, known-vulnerable framework, and only npm was audited. The fix is right: move fastapi to a release that allows starlette>=0.49.1 and add an explicit `starlette>=0.49.1` floor. Performance is better, with no runtime cost.

confirmed.title: Frontend Docker build fails on a fresh clone because /app/public is not in git
confirmed.evidence: `git ls-tree -r --name-only 62b22d6` lists no frontend/public/* entries. On the author's machine, frontend/public exists but is empty and untracked, and git cannot track empty directories. The runtime stage runs `COPY --from=build /app/public ./public`. On a clean checkout, CI runner or server, `docker compose up --build` (README.md:8) stops with `failed to compute cache key: "/app/public": not found`. It only works locally because the empty directory happens to exist.
confirmed.fix: In frontend/Dockerfile line 8, change to `RUN mkdir -p public && npm run build`. Alternatively, commit `frontend/public/.gitkeep`, but that file is then served publicly at /.gitkeep.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Neutral.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed. `git ls-tree -r 62b22d6` has no frontend/public entries. Locally, frontend/public exists but is empty and untracked, and git cannot track an empty directory. frontend/Dockerfile:15 `COPY --from=build /app/public ./public` fails when the source path does not exist, and `next build` does not create public/. So the documented `docker compose up --build` (README) breaks on any clean checkout or CI runner. I lowered it to medium: it stops deployment outright but is easy to diagnose and has no security or data impact. `RUN mkdir -p public && npm run build` is the smallest fix. Performance is neutral.

confirmed.title: Next rewrite proxy cuts upload bodies off at 10 MB, so uploads between 10 and 50 MB always fail
confirmed.evidence: The browser posts FormData to the relative `/api/content` (library/page.tsx:219-223, lib/api.ts:27), so every upload goes through the Next rewrite. For external rewrites, router-server.js:417 calls `proxyRequest(..., getRequestMeta(req,'clonableBody').cloneBodyStream(), ...)`. That body comes from `getCloneableBody(req, config.experimental.proxyClientMaxBodySize)` (resolve-routes.js:124-125), and the default is 10485760 (config-shared.js:279; body-streams.js:30). Past that size, cloneBodyStream stops pushing data and logs `Request body exceeded 10 MB ... Only the first 10 MB will be available`. httpxy still forwards the original Content-Length header. As a result, uvicorn receives a truncated multipart body and waits until the 30 s proxyTimeout (proxy-request.js:37) or a disconnect. The backend says it accepts 50 MB (main.py:18, 131), and the seed data includes 28 MB and 184 MB items, so the 50 MB limit cannot be reached through the UI. A second effect: the unread `p2` Readable in body-streams.js keeps every chunk, up to the limit, in Node memory for each in-flight POST.
confirmed.fix: Match the two limits. Either add `experimental: { proxyClientMaxBodySize: "51mb" }` in next.config.ts (50 MB plus multipart overhead), or lower MAX_UPLOAD in main.py to 10 MB if that is enough for the product.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Raising the Next limit makes things worse: each in-flight upload then holds up to about 51 MB in Node, on top of the 50 MB Python already reads into memory (SEC-6). Pair it with container mem_limit. Lowering MAX_UPLOAD to 10 MB is better for memory on both tiers.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed against next 16.3.6. resolve-routes.js:124-125 wraps every non-upgrade request with getCloneableBody(req, config.experimental.proxyClientMaxBodySize), whose default is 10485760 (config-shared.js:279). router-server.js:417 proxies external rewrites with `cloneBodyStream()`. In body-streams.js:95-106, once the limit is passed it logs a warning and ends both p1 and p2, so only part of the body reaches the proxy. httpxy setupOutgoing copies `{...req.headers}`, including the original Content-Length, so uvicorn waits for bytes that never arrive until the 30 s proxyTimeout (proxy-request.js:37) and the upload fails. The browser uploads through the relative `/api/content` path (lib/api.ts:27, library/page.tsx:219-222), and main.py:18/131 advertise 50 MB, so the 10-50 MB range can never succeed. The memory point is also correct: p2 is a Readable that is pushed to and never read, so it holds up to the limit per in-flight request. Both proposed fixes are valid. Lowering MAX_UPLOAD to 10 MB is the cheaper one and is better for memory.

confirmed.title: Compose services have no memory/pid limits, log rotation, read-only root FS or dropped capabilities, and the frontend has no healthcheck
confirmed.evidence: Neither service sets mem_limit, pids_limit, read_only, cap_drop or security_opt, and neither sets `logging` options. Docker's default json-file driver keeps logs without limit, and uvicorn logs one access line per request with no rate limiting (SEC-5). The frontend service (lines 15-25) has no healthcheck, so `restart: unless-stopped` never fires for a hung Next process. Combined with SEC-6 (50 MB in memory per upload) and the Next per-request body buffer above, a burst of uploads uses up host RAM instead of being contained by a cgroup.
confirmed.fix: For each service, add: `mem_limit: 512m`, `pids_limit: 256`, `cap_drop: [ALL]`, `security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]`, `read_only: true`, `logging: {driver: json-file, options: {max-size: "10m", max-file: "3"}}`. The backend also needs `tmpfs: ["/tmp:size=128m"]`, because starlette moves uploads over 1 MB to /tmp, while /data stays on the volume. For the frontend, add a healthcheck: `["CMD","node","-e","fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1),()=>process.exit(1))"]`. The frontend works with read_only because it uses no next/image or ISR cache writes.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Better isolation: an upload burst OOM-kills and restarts one container instead of slowing the whole host. The tmpfs makes spooled uploads RAM-backed, which is faster but counts against mem_limit, so size the two together.
confirmed.verify_note: Partly holds. docker-compose.yml (baseline) does have no mem_limit, pids_limit or logging options. A per-container memory cap is a distinct, useful containment step for the known SEC-6 (50 MB read per upload) and for the Next per-request buffer above, and log rotation bounds disk growth under SEC-5. One part is wrong: the frontend healthcheck rationale. Plain Docker and Compose (not Swarm) never restart a container for being `unhealthy`; `restart: unless-stopped` acts only when the process exits. Adding a healthcheck would therefore not restart a hung Next process, so drop that part or pair it with an external autoheal. Whether json-file logs grow without limit depends on the host's daemon.json. cap_drop, no-new-privileges and read_only are generic defense-in-depth that sit next to SEC-10. Keep the finding at low, scoped to mem_limit and log rotation. If read_only is applied to the backend, the tmpfs for /tmp is required: starlette spools uploads over 1 MB there.

confirmed.title: SEC-10 fix pitfall: a non-root backend will fail on the existing root-owned `data` volume, and the healthcheck will not catch it
confirmed.evidence: `VOLUME /data` (Dockerfile:7) is backed by the named volume `data` (docker-compose.yml:6-7). Today's container runs as root, so it has already created app.db and uploads/ as root-owned files. Docker copies image ownership into a named volume only when the volume is empty on first mount. If `USER app` is added, the existing deployment opens app.db read-only and cannot create app.db-journal in the root-owned /data. Every write route then fails with `attempt to write a readonly database` or PermissionError. The healthcheck calls /api/health (main.py:93-95), which does not touch the DB or the volume, so the container still reports healthy.
confirmed.fix: Before VOLUME: `RUN useradd -r -u 10001 app && mkdir -p /data && chown app /data`, then `USER app`. For existing deployments, run `docker compose run --rm -u 0 backend chown -R 10001 /data` once. Optionally have /api/health run `SELECT 1` and check that DATA is writable with `os.access(DATA, os.W_OK)`.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Neutral.
confirmed.verify_note: I reproduced the core claim in the scratchpad with a 555 directory and a 444 app.db that already had the tables. sqlite3.connect falls back to read-only, and init()'s `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` plus `SELECT 1 FROM content` succeed, so startup works. The first INSERT then raises `OperationalError: attempt to write a readonly database`. /api/health (main.py:93-95) touches neither the DB nor /data, so the container keeps reporting healthy while every write route returns 500. Docker copies image ownership into a named volume only when the volume is empty on first mount, so existing deployments keep their root-owned files. This is useful guidance for applying the known SEC-10 fix rather than a standalone vulnerability, hence info. The proposed chown in the Dockerfile plus a one-time chown of the volume is correct.

confirmed.title: SEC-5 fix pitfall: behind the Next rewrite the backend never sees the client IP, and a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For passes through unchanged
confirmed.evidence: Next's rewrite proxy builds httpxy without `xfwd` (proxy-request.js:31-41) and only injects `x-forwarded-host`. Other request headers are copied as-is, including any X-Forwarded-For the attacker sends (httpxy setupOutgoing `e.headers={...r.headers}`). Next's own `x-forwarded-for` default is set only in base-server.js:612, on the render path, not the rewrite path. uvicorn trusts forwarded headers only from 127.0.0.1 (config.py:333). So a per-IP limiter added in main.py would see one IP, the frontend container, for all users and throttle everyone together. If it is switched to trust X-Forwarded-For, it can be bypassed, both because Next forwards the spoofed value and because port 8011 is published (SEC-10).
confirmed.fix: Do IP-keyed rate limiting at the component that sees the TCP peer: a reverse proxy in front of 3011 that overwrites X-Forwarded-For. Make the backend trust only that proxy (`--forwarded-allow-ips=<proxy ip>`), and stop publishing 8011.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Better: rejected requests are dropped at the edge before reaching Node or Python, instead of being parsed by both tiers.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed. proxy-request.js:30-41 builds ProxyServer without `xfwd`, and httpxy's web-path xfwd middleware returns early with `if(!r.xfwd)return`. setupOutgoing copies `{...r.headers}`, so an attacker's X-Forwarded-For is forwarded as-is. Next's INTERNAL_HEADERS filter (server-ipc/utils.js:62-74) does not strip it, and Next sets its own `x-forwarded-for ??=` only in base-server.js:612 (the render path). uvicorn's forwarded_allow_ips defaults to 127.0.0.1 (config.py:333), so in Compose the backend sees the frontend container IP for every user. A per-IP limiter added in main.py would therefore throttle everyone together, or could be bypassed if configured to trust XFF, especially with 8011 published. This is a valid pitfall to note when fixing SEC-5, hence info. The proposed fix is correct: limit at an edge proxy that overwrites XFF, trust only that proxy, and stop publishing 8011.

confirmed.title: async def create_content runs blocking sqlite and a 50MB disk write on the event loop, so it can freeze the whole API for up to 5s
confirmed.evidence: create_content is declared `async def` (L123). That means `(UPLOADS / fname).write_bytes(blob)` (L133, up to 50MB), `with db() as con:` with INSERT plus an fsync commit (L135-137), and get_or_404's correlated COUNT scans (L138) all run synchronously on uvicorn's single event loop. Every other endpoint is a sync `def` and runs in the threadpool. If another connection holds the sqlite write lock, sqlite3's default 5s busy timeout sleeps on the loop and stalls every in-flight request. Measured on a scratch copy of the 62b22d6 main.py (DATA_DIR in scratch), with a second connection holding BEGIN IMMEDIATE for 4s: GET /api/health took 0.025s while the sync `approve` waited on the lock, and 3.789s while `create_content` waited. After the fix below, the same probe gave health 0.010s and a 3MB upload still returned 201.
confirmed.fix: Make it a sync endpoint so FastAPI runs it in the threadpool. Change L123 `async def create_content(` to `def create_content(` and L129 `blob = await file.read(MAX_UPLOAD + 1)` to `blob = file.file.read(MAX_UPLOAD + 1)`. Form parsing still happens asynchronously before the call (fastapi/routing.py:247).
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Pure performance gain: the loop never blocks on disk or sqlite. It also removes a DoS amplifier, because unauthenticated writes (SEC-1/SEC-5) that hold the lock can no longer freeze unrelated requests and health checks.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed. At 62b22d6, main.py:123 is the only `async def` route. FastAPI awaits a coroutine endpoint directly on the loop (fastapi/routing.py:211-214 run_endpoint_function); only sync defs go to run_in_threadpool. That puts write_bytes (L133, up to 50MB), sqlite INSERT/commit (L135-137, Python's default 5s busy timeout) and get_or_404's COUNTs (L138) on the event loop. SEC-6 covers only memory, so this is not already known. The fix is valid: Starlette seeks each spooled file back to 0 after parsing (formparsers.py:265), so `file.file.read(MAX_UPLOAD + 1)` in a sync def reads the same bytes, and the form is still parsed and closed asynchronously in routing.py:247-248.

confirmed.title: Correction to SEC-6: the 50MB cap runs only after Starlette has spooled the entire request body to disk, so request size is unbounded
confirmed.evidence: FastAPI parses the whole form with `body = await request.form()` (fastapi/routing.py:247) before any dependency or endpoint code runs. Starlette's MultiPartParser rolls file parts to a temp file after 1MB (formparsers.py:124 `spool_max_size`) and applies no size limit to file parts; `max_part_size` covers only non-file fields (formparsers.py:159-166). The `len(blob) > MAX_UPLOAD` check at L129-131 therefore runs after the full body is on disk in the container's temp dir. Measured against the baseline main.py: a 200MB multipart POST returned 413 only after the server had accepted all 200,000,527 bytes (8.2s). Port 8011 is published (SEC-10), so a proxy cap in Next would not cover it anyway.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Better overall. Oversized uploads are refused before any disk or network I/O, instead of after writing up to many GB to the temp dir. The cost is one header check per request, which is negligible.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed in library source. FastAPI calls `await request.form()` before the endpoint runs (routing.py:247). Starlette's MultiPartParser enforces max_part_size only when `self._current_part.file is None`; file parts are appended to _file_parts_to_write with no limit (formparsers.py:159-166) and roll to disk after spool_max_size=1MB. Neither uvicorn nor python-multipart caps the body, and port 8011 is published directly. So L129-131 bounds only how much is read into memory, not how much is received and written to temp disk. That is materially new relative to SEC-6 (memory) and SEC-5 (rate). A typical SEC-6 fix that streams with a cap would still not close it. Notes on the proposed fix: @app.middleware creates a BaseHTTPMiddleware, which carries per-request overhead, so a few-line pure-ASGI check or a reverse-proxy client_max_body_size is leaner. The 413 it returns also bypasses CORSMiddleware headers, which is harmless because the browser goes through the same-origin Next proxy.

confirmed.title: Correction to PERF-3: the obvious events(content_id,type) index alone makes the analytics 'recent' query slower, and per-item COUNT stays O(events per item)
confirmed.evidence:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN runs on a scratch copy of the baseline schema with 200k events (min of 3 runs; the host was heavily loaded, so the plans and ratios are the signal):
(1) `recent` (L204-205, `ORDER BY e.ts DESC, e.rowid DESC LIMIT 8`): with no index it plans SCAN e + TEMP B-TREE at 1359ms. With only ev_ct(content_id,type) the plan becomes 'SCAN e USING INDEX ev_ct' + TEMP B-TREE at 5059ms, 3.7x worse; at 1M events it went from 5.1s to 32.7s. Adding events(ts) makes it 0.1ms, but an events(ts,type) index does not satisfy ORDER BY ts, rowid, and the plan falls back to ev_ct at 4203ms.
(2) `daily` (L197): a plain events(ts) index gives a non-covering range scan with no gain over a table scan (3511ms vs 2974ms). events(ts,type) gives 'SEARCH events USING COVERING INDEX'.
(3) The correlated COUNTs in ROW (L82-83) are O(k) even with the covering ev_ct index. ROW-by-id took 0.3ms for an item with 1.9k events and 26-50ms for one with 102k events. The events table is append-only and unauthenticated writes are allowed (SEC-1), so a single hot item makes every list, analytics, detail and track call slower over time.
confirmed.fix: In init() add `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ev_ct ON events(content_id, type); CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ev_tt ON events(ts, type);`. Change L205 to `ORDER BY e.ts DESC LIMIT 8`, which makes 'recent' a backward index scan: measured 0.1ms, no temp B-tree. Within the same second, ties order by type then rowid. If events keep growing, follow up with `views`/`shares` counter columns on content, incremented in track(), so ROW stops counting entirely.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Two indexes add a small write cost to each event insert. That cost is far outweighed by read cost that becomes O(log n). Counter columns would cap the read amplification an attacker can cause through unauthenticated event writes.
confirmed.verify_note: Reproduced on a scratch in-memory DB (sqlite 3.45.1, same as the venv) with the baseline schema and 200k events. No index: 'SCAN e' + TEMP B-TREE, 195ms. With ev_ct(content_id,type) only, the planner switches to 'SCAN e USING INDEX ev_ct' + TEMP B-TREE at 420ms, about 2x worse. Adding ev_tt(ts,type) leaves the original ORDER BY ts DESC, rowid DESC on ev_ct (437ms). Dropping the rowid tie-break uses ev_tt with no temp B-tree (~0ms). This is a valid, materially new correction: the obvious fix for the known index gap regresses this query. A smaller alternative also measured ~0ms: an index on events(ts) alone satisfies the existing `ORDER BY e.ts DESC, e.rowid DESC`, because the rowid is the implicit last index column, so the query text and its tie order can stay unchanged. Severity is lowered because the seeded data is about 2k events and the UI only adds share events, so the regression matters only at large event volumes.

confirmed.title: Animated aurora with filter: blur(80px) under six backdrop-filter surfaces keeps the landing hero re-rasterizing every frame, indefinitely
confirmed.evidence: `.aurora` (L170-176) applies `filter: blur(80px)` to a container at inset:-20%, which is 140% x 140% of the hero section. Its three 35-45vmax children animate transform forever (L182 `drift 18s infinite alternate`). Because the children move, the 80px blur has to be recomputed on every frame. On top of it in Hero (app/page.tsx) are six backdrop-filter surfaces that re-sample the changing backdrop each frame: the eyebrow `.glass` pill (L24, blur(24px) saturate(180%)), the tilting device `.glass` card (L47), and four stat cells with `backdrop-blur` (L81, 8px) over an 80%-opaque background, where the blur is barely visible. A second infinite aurora runs inside the Demo card (L264). The page never goes idle while the hero or Demo is on screen, which costs GPU time and battery on the phones the product targets. This is a code-level finding: I did not trace it, because the host was saturated. Confirm with DevTools > Rendering > Frame Rendering Stats.
confirmed.fix: Remove the per-frame blur by baking the falloff into each span: delete `filter: blur(80px);` from `.aurora` and give each span a radial gradient instead of a solid fill, e.g. `.aurora span:nth-child(1){background:radial-gradient(closest-side,var(--accent),transparent)}`, with the same for -2 and -3. The animation becomes transform-only, so the compositor can handle it cheaply. Also drop `backdrop-blur` from the stat cells at app/page.tsx:81; their 80% background already hides the backdrop.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: No security impact. Removes continuous GPU blur work and five of the hero's backdrop-filter passes.
confirmed.verify_note: The code matches the claim. globals.css:170-186 has `.aurora{inset:-20%;filter:blur(80px)}` over three 35-45vmax spans running `drift 18s infinite alternate`, so the filtered surface's content changes every frame and the large-radius blur is re-applied continuously. page.tsx:20 and page.tsx:264 use it. Backdrop-filter surfaces at page.tsx:24, 47 and 81 sit over it, and the `.float` wrapper keeps the glass card moving as well. The only mitigation is the prefers-reduced-motion rule (globals.css:274), which helps only users who opt in. This is a well-known continuous GPU cost, and replacing the blur with radial-gradient spans is the standard visually equivalent fix. Severity is low because it was not traced or measured and affects only the landing page.

confirmed.title: num()/date() build a new Intl formatter on every call, inside render hot paths; the Library re-renders every card on each keystroke
confirmed.evidence:
`num` (L283-284) and `date` (L286-287) call `new Intl.NumberFormat(...)` and `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(...)` on every call. Hot callers:
- Library: each card calls n() three times and date() once (library/page.tsx:81,89,91-92). Cards are inline, not memoized, so each `setQ` keystroke (L58) re-renders every card synchronously before the 180ms debounce, and the list is unbounded (PERF-5).
- CountUp: re-renders and formats on every rAF frame for 1.1s per counter (components/ui.tsx:95-103); 5 on the dashboard, 1 in the hero.
- AreaChart: on each hover index change, 2 NumberFormat plus 1 DateTimeFormat constructions (Charts.tsx:31,34).
Measured in Node 24 (same V8/ICU as Chrome) with fa-IR: constructing NumberFormat was ~40x slower than reusing one, and DateTimeFormat ~35x. A 200-card render cost 1369ms uncached vs 15ms cached, about 90x. The host was heavily loaded, so absolute times are inflated about 15x and the ratio is the signal; an unloaded desktop is roughly 90ms of formatter construction per keystroke at 200 items, and a phone several times that.
confirmed.fix: Cache the formatters in i18n.tsx: `const nf = new Map<string, Intl.NumberFormat>(); export const num = (n: number, lang: Lang, opts?: Intl.NumberFormatOptions) => { const k = lang + JSON.stringify(opts ?? {}); let f = nf.get(k); if (!f) nf.set(k, (f = new Intl.NumberFormat(lang === "fa" ? "fa-IR" : "en-US", opts))); return f.format(n); };`. Apply the same pattern to `date` with a DateTimeFormat map. Callers do not change.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: No security impact. Removes most per-render formatting cost across the dashboard, library and charts.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed: i18n.tsx (baseline lines ~283-287) builds `new Intl.NumberFormat` and `new Intl.DateTimeFormat` on every call. Library cards are inline with no memo, so each setQ keystroke re-renders all cards before the debounce, at four formatter constructions per card (library/page.tsx:81,89,91,92). CountUp formats on every rAF frame (ui.tsx), and AreaChart formats on every hover change. At today's 9 seed items the cost is a few ms. It grows linearly with the unbounded list (PERF-5), and reusing formatters is the documented Intl best practice. The proposed memoized num/date is correct and needs no caller changes. Valid low-severity finding.

confirmed.title: Detail actions and download call get_or_404, which runs two correlated COUNT scans just to check that the row exists (twice per track/approve/new_version)
confirmed.evidence: get_or_404 (L86-90) always runs ROW, which computes two correlated COUNT(*) subqueries over events. It serves as a bare existence check in track (L167), approve (L157), new_version (L148), delete (L184) and the public download (L175, which only needs file/title_en). track, approve and new_version then call it again to build the response, so a single POST /events/view runs four COUNTs plus an insert. Unindexed at 200k events, one ROW-by-id took 108-123ms; with an index it is still O(events for that item), 26-50ms for a hot item. The frontend also discards the POST response: share() and approve call POST, then GET /content/{id} through refresh(), then GET /content through load() (library/page.tsx:135,141-142,174,106). Each click therefore runs the count work three or more times.
confirmed.fix: Skip the counts on existence checks: `def get_or_404(con, cid, counts=True):\n    row = con.execute(ROW + " WHERE c.id=?" if counts else "SELECT * FROM content WHERE id=?", (cid,)).fetchone()`. Pass `counts=False` at L148, L157, L167, L175 and L184. Keep the default for the final response calls.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Halves the per-request scan work on the unauthenticated event-write path (SEC-1/SEC-5 amplification) and removes it entirely from the public download path (SEC-2).
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed. get_or_404 (main.py:86-90) always runs ROW, which has two correlated COUNT(*) over events. It is used only as an existence or field lookup at L148 (needs version), L157, L167, L175 (needs file/title_en) and L184 (needs file), and track, approve and new_version call it twice. The frontend then discards the POST body and runs refresh() (GET /content/{id}) plus load() (GET /content) (library/page.tsx:135,141-142,174,106). The fix is correct (`ROW + ' WHERE c.id=?' if counts else ...` binds as intended), and every skipped call site uses only content columns. This is distinct from PERF-2 (analytics) and PERF-3 (indexes). Severity is low: at about 2k seeded events each COUNT is sub-ms, and the cost grows mainly through unauthenticated event writes.

confirmed.title: Library search fetches are never aborted, so a slower stale response can overwrite newer results
confirmed.evidence: The debounce effect (L24) clears only the timer. A request already sent is never cancelled, and `load` (L19-22) applies whichever response arrives last via `setItems`. A broader query such as 'a' matches more rows, so its correlated-count work takes longer than a later, narrower 'ab' and can resolve after it, leaving the grid showing stale results. `t` is also in load's deps (L22) although only the error toast uses it, so every language toggle triggers an extra full-list fetch.
confirmed.fix: Pass an AbortSignal through. In load use `(signal?: AbortSignal) => api<Content[]>(`/content?${p}`, { signal }).then(setItems).catch((e) => { if (e.name !== "AbortError") { setItems([]); toast(t.lib.error, "err"); } })`, and make the effect `useEffect(() => { const ac = new AbortController(); const id = setTimeout(() => load(ac.signal), 180); return () => { clearTimeout(id); ac.abort(); }; }, [load]);`. api() already spreads `init` into fetch.
confirmed.perf_tie_in: Neutral for security. Saves client work and bandwidth. The backend's sync handler still finishes its query after a disconnect, so server-side savings need the index/counter fixes.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed. library/page.tsx:19-24: the effect cleanup clears only the timer. A request already in flight is never aborted, and setItems applies whichever response arrives last, the classic out-of-order race across q, category and status changes. `t` is in load's deps (L22) and changes on a language toggle (t = dict[lang]), which triggers an extra list fetch. The 180ms debounce and fast backend make the race unlikely today, but it is a real correctness bug. The fix is correct: api() spreads init into fetch (api.ts:27), an aborted fetch rejects with name 'AbortError', and other callers of load() pass no signal, which still works.

rejected.title: Approve is not tied to the version the reviewer saw and doesn't require pending status (TOCTOU)
rejected.reason: The race is in the code, but it has no impact today. new_version() (main.py:145-151) changes only the note and version number. The stored file and every other content field stay the same, so a reviewer who 'approves v3 without seeing it' is approving byte-identical content. The finding itself admits it only matters once versions carry files, so it is speculative. Re-approving an already approved item only bumps updated_at, which is cosmetic. The real root problem, versions not carrying content, is already captured under the approval-gate finding.

rejected.title: Deleting an item also erases its view/share history, and approvals record no one
rejected.reason: The lines are accurate (main.py:185-187, 158), but the security claim depends on identities that don't exist. With no users (SEC-1) there is no actor to record, and the insider scenario only appears after auth is built. Today this is a generic audit-log feature request that belongs in the SEC-1 design, not a separate concrete issue. Cascading the delete is consistent with a hard delete. Its one concrete side effect, past days on the dashboard series dropping after a delete, is analytics behaviour the finding doesn't argue.

rejected.title: Low impact: the internal stored filename is returned in every content response
rejected.reason: It's true that ROW selects c.* (main.py:82), so `file` (cid + extension) is returned. But there is no static /uploads mount, the path can't be influenced, and every file can already be downloaded anonymously by id (SEC-2). Revealing the extension adds no exposure beyond SEC-2 and SEC-3. It is a data-minimisation nicety, not a finding.

rejected.title: The rewrite proxy passes the client's X-Forwarded-For through unchanged and never adds the real client IP, so per-IP controls see one address or a spoofable one
rejected.reason: The facts are right: proxy-request.js does not set xfwd, and httpxy copies the client's headers as they arrive. But nothing in the baseline reads them. main.py never uses request.client, X-Forwarded-For or X-Forwarded-Proto. Uvicorn 0.32.1 trusts forwarded headers only from 127.0.0.1 by default (config.py:333), and the Dockerfile CMD does not change that, so a spoofed XFF/XFP from a client has no effect today. Forwarding Cookie on a same-origin rewrite is expected behaviour, and the only cookie is the non-sensitive lang cookie. The finding only matters if someone later adds a per-IP limiter (SEC-5) and trusts the wrong header. That makes it design advice for that future fix, not a defect in the code as it stands. The backend is also published directly on 8011 (SEC-10), so any limit put only in the proxy could be bypassed anyway, which is already covered.

rejected.title: frontend/.dockerignore does not exclude .env*, and Next standalone copies .env and .env.production into the runtime image
rejected.reason: The mechanism is real: build/index.js:325-333 copies loaded `.env` and `.env.production` into .next/standalone. But nothing is at risk today. The frontend directory has no .env* files (only next-env.d.ts), and the frontend uses no secrets: its only setting is BACKEND_URL, passed as a build ARG. The `.env*` line in frontend/.gitignore:34 is the create-next-app default, not a sign that secrets exist. .env.local is not copied into standalone, and NEXT_PUBLIC_* inlining is public by design. This is purely theoretical, so it is not a finding.

rejected.title: SQLite stays in rollback-journal mode with synchronous=FULL, so every write is a multi-fsync commit that serializes writers and blocks readers
rejected.reason: This is generic tuning advice, not a defect. DELETE journal with synchronous=FULL is SQLite's safe default. The premise that every track() view or share is a frequent write does not hold: the frontend never posts view events (the only events/ caller is library/page.tsx:141, share). The other writes (approve, version, upload, delete, demo) are rare, explicit user actions. In rollback mode, readers are blocked only during the commit's PENDING/EXCLUSIVE window, not for the whole transaction. The 109ms/commit figure was measured on a saturated host. The only realistic pressure is an unauthenticated write flood, which is SEC-1/SEC-5 territory. WAL is a fine optional tweak, but the finding shows no concrete issue at this app's write rate.

rejected.title: Hero tilt calls setState with a new object on every pointermove, re-rendering the whole Hero
rejected.reason: The behavior is accurate (page.tsx:16, 41-44), but the impact is negligible. Hero is a small, fixed tree of roughly 40 nodes, so reconciling it per pointermove is sub-ms, and it only happens while a mouse moves over the device card. CountUp's effect depends only on [value] (ui.tsx), so re-renders do not restart its animation. The expensive part is the transform change on the backdrop-filtered `.glass` card, and the proposed CSS-variable fix still changes that transform on every pointermove. So the GPU cost stays the same and only a trivial React render is saved. This is micro-optimization padding.

rejected.title: Each Library card's version badge uses .glass, adding one backdrop-filter surface per card over a static gradient
rejected.reason: The code matches (library/page.tsx:80 uses `glass` with !bg-black/20), but the cost claim is not established. The badges are tiny, about 60x24px. Browsers only draw backdrop filters for on-screen cards, so an unbounded list does not mean N concurrent passes; only the handful of visible cards count. Blur cost scales with area, so these are cheap compared with the sticky header and toolbar layers that are already there. The effect is also not visually a no-op: saturate(180%) changes the badge's tint. This is unmeasured micro-optimization.
